title: Let Us Connect Hearts with Empathy

sections.title: What Does Speaking After Thinking Mean?
content: Usually it is said not to respond immediately when in emotion. Even though that suggestion is useful, if it is not known what kind of examination should happen in the mind, that pause alone may not be enough. In the introductory introduction it was explained that the Nonviolent Communication method being learned in this series provides a path for that inner examination. When an event happens, knowing the differences of what we saw, what commentary we made about it, what feeling arose in us, and what need is behind that feeling is the foundation for conversation.

When we immediately understand the word the other person said as ‘I was insulted,’ our response revolves only around that judgment. If we come to know which pain, which fear that same word touched in us, another choice becomes visible to us. Likewise opportunity is also formed to listen to what need is behind the other person’s words. This is not forcibly suppressing anger; it is knowing what is being indicated in us through anger.

sections.title: Why Do We Hesitate to State Our Needs?
content: Clearly stating the need that is in the mind is not easy in many contexts. According to the speaker’s explanation, there may be fear that if we express the need others will regard us as selfish. There may also be worry that they will not respond to our word, or fear that they will directly reject it. These make us remain without saying the matter we need. In some contexts we hope that the other person will understand without our stating the need; when that does not happen dissatisfaction increases.

Recognizing these fears does not mean seeing them as wrong. The responses faced earlier when the need was stated may have increased caution in us. Observing such caution, stating our need not as a demand imposed on the other person but as a respectful request is an important practice in NVC. Even if the other person says ‘no’ to the request, there is no need for the conversation to end. The need behind that ‘no’ can also be listened to.

sections.title: Feelings, Needs, Judgments — Three Different Levels
content: When pain has arisen in us it is easy to say ‘they are not caring for me.’ But that may be an interpretation we made on a person’s behavior. Behind it there may be loneliness, disappointment, affection, or the need for recognition. If we express only the judgment the other person may try to defend themselves; when we clearly state our feeling and need, space may form for mutual understanding.

In the same way, while listening to others’ words too, without stopping only with the decision ‘they are speaking wrongly,’ it is necessary to know what pain is in their experience. This is not agreeing with their every word. Even though there is disagreement, respecting their human need is possible. This difference is very important in listening with empathy.

sections.title: Empathy in Marshall Rosenberg’s Story
content: In the discourse a story related to Marshall Rosenberg’s mediation experience came for mention. The speaker explained that in a meeting he faced severe criticisms because he was an American. Instead of immediately counter-arguing those criticisms, it was said that he tried to listen to the pain caused by war, fear, and insecure conditions in the lives of those speaking angrily.

What is important in this story is not the words used in the criticisms; it is the effort to recognize the pain behind them. When someone is intensely blaming, the ordinary response is defending our intentions or finding fault with them. What the speaker explained as the path Rosenberg showed is only trying to understand what security need, what human suffering is behind their anger. When listened to in that way, the person in the conflict also has the opportunity to state their experience more clearly.

This incident should be seen as a general principle: **there is no need to defend against criticism; it is possible to listen to the pain behind the criticism.** The place, persons, and historical details related to the story should be further confirmed with the original video before publication.

sections.title: Empathy Does Not Mean Immediately Giving Advice
content: When a person close to us states pain, it feels as though a solution should be suggested immediately. Words such as ‘it should be done that way,’ ‘think like this,’ ‘that is not a big problem’ may come with good intention, yet the opportunity for that person to fully state their experience may decrease. The speaker specially mentioned listening with empathy in this context. First giving space to the other person’s words, understanding the feeling they are experiencing, and trying to listen to what their need is are necessary.

When someone is in pain, the attention we give may be more valuable than the answer we say. If the listening person is able to set aside their decisions for a short while, the speaking person may also observe the experience within themselves newly. This listening is not passive; it is a living relationship that remains with attention, patience, and without judgment.

sections.title: Personal Experience with Dr. Newton
content: The speaker shared an experience that arose for her with Dr. Newton. She explained that when he listened to her words without judgment and with full attention, even though he did not specially state a solution, a new understanding arose in her. Through this example it was conveyed that empathy is not always giving an answer to our problem from outside.

Sometimes because of the experience that someone is listening to our words peacefully, we ourselves are able to see our situation from a new angle. What we need, what is paining us becomes clear. The speaker used this experience as an example of the effect of empathy. In this appears the suggestion that not only remembering the guru with respect, but also practicing that listening quality in our daily relationships.

sections.title: How Do Childhood Messages Influence Our Conversation?
content: The manner of expressing our feelings is not merely a habit formed today. The speaker explained that the messages heard while growing up in the family and in society influence our responses. Messages such as ‘girls should not get angry,’ ‘boys should not cry,’ ‘one should not ask so much’ may stand as obstacles even to recognizing feelings. With the fear that if a feeling is expressed it may not be accepted, we may hide it.

However, by hiding feelings we lose the information they tell about our needs. If we are able to recognize pain we can ask questions of whether we need comfort, respect, rest, or connection. In the same way, without seeing another’s tears only as weakness or anger only as wrong, we can know in what experience that person is. This change begins from small family conversations.

sections.title: Respect in Request, Freedom in Answer
content: Stating our need and pressuring another person to listen to our word are not the same. In conversation with empathy, while clearly asking what we need, the other person’s situation should also be respected. If they do not agree, listening to what limitation or need they have at that time is useful rather than deciding them as loveless persons.

This viewpoint is specially needed in family relationships. Just as the desire that our word should be heard is natural, the need that the other person also should have their feelings heard is equally natural. If in the effort to fulfill one person’s need the other person’s need is completely neglected, dissatisfaction remains in the relationship. If both persons’ needs can be recognized in the same conversation, new paths for the problem may become visible.

sections.title: Even Though There Is Difference, Connection Is Possible
content: Empathy does not say that everyone should come to the same opinion. Even if our opinions are different, we can understand the matters important to each other. If anger is visible in someone’s words, behind it there may be the need for safety or respect. Even if rejection is visible in another’s silence, behind it there may be the need for time or clarity. These are not matters to be decided beforehand; they are to be known through listening.

That is why empathy is more than a conversation method. It is the effort we make to see the person in front of us not as a ‘problem’ but as a human being with feelings and needs. When such a vision forms we also become ready to express our needs without blames.

sections.title: Empathy as Daily Practice
content: The practical direction emerging from this discourse is clear: before responding immediately to a word one should observe what feeling arose in us; one should come to know what need is behind that feeling; one should try to listen to such a need in the other person’s words as well. Thereafter our request should be stated as clearly and respectfully as possible. Even if we are unable to do this process completely all at once, every conversation becomes a practice opportunity.

Just as through meditation we have learned to observe the movements within us, in relationships too we can learn to observe the difference among feelings, judgments, and needs. **Listening, understanding, and expressing the need with respect** — this teaching reminds us that these three actions take us in the direction of increasing peace in our words.
